activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Aaron ran to the playground. He wanted his little blue car. He looked in his pocket. The car was not there.

"Where did you go?" Aaron asked. His teacher, Miss Kim, came over. "Retracing your steps," she said. "Go back to each place you went, in order."

Aaron thought hard. First he had gone to the swings. He walked back to the swings. He looked under the seat. No car. Next he had gone down the slide. He walked to the slide. He looked at the bottom. No car. Last he had played in the sandbox. He ran to the sandbox. There, in the sand, was the blue car!

"I found it!" Aaron said. He held it up high. Miss Kim clapped. "Let the car ride down the slide," she said. Aaron set the car at the top. It zoomed down. Aaron laughed and chased it across the cloudy sky's little shadow on the ground.

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Asher skipped to the sink. It was snack time at summer camp. His team sat at a cozy table with apple slices.

Asher turned on the water. He rubbed his hands fast. But there were no bubbles. He looked and looked. Not one bubble.

He called to his friend Maya. "Look at my hands. No bubbles!"

Maya held up her hands. They were full of white bubbles. "I used soap," she said.

Asher found the soap bottle. He put one pump on his hands. He rubbed and rubbed the soap and water together. Bubbles! Lots of bubbles! They popped on his fingers.

"Bubbles, bubbles, bubbles," he sang.

He counted to twenty with Maya. Then he rinsed and dried his hands. His hands were clean and warm.

Asher picked up an apple slice. "I love bubbles," he said. He took a big, happy bite.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Mya stood in the storytime room. The rug had striped pillows on it. Today Mya would get her first library card.

The librarian smiled at her. "Sign your name here," she said. Mya wrote the letters, one by one. M, Y, A. The card was blue and shiny.

"Now you can borrow a book," said the librarian. Mya wanted a book about trucks. She looked on the shelf. She saw a book about bears. She saw a book about paint. No trucks. She looked again. Still no trucks.

Mya tapped her chin. Then she walked back to the librarian. "Can you help me find trucks?" she asked.

"I help people find books," said the librarian. "That is my job. Let's look together." They walked to the other side of the room. The librarian pulled out a big red book. It was all about trucks!

Mya hugged the book. "I did it," she said. "My first book."

The other kids began to clap. Mya held up her card and her truck book. "One card, one book, one happy day," said Mya. The librarian laughed and stamped the book. "Bring it back next week," she said, "and we'll find two."

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Luka sat on the big chair at the doctor's office. He wanted to be brave today. The nurse came in with a tray. "Let's check you all over," she said.

First, Luka used his eyes to see the tray. He saw a small light, a sticker, and a lemon slice. Next, he used his ears to hear the doctor knock. Knock, knock. Then Luka used his nose to smell the lemon. "Does it smell like orange juice?" he asked. "Smell it and see," said the nurse. Luka sniffed. It smelled sharp and lemony.

"Now touch the cotton ball," said the nurse. Luka used his fingers to touch it. It was soft like a cloud. "Last thing," said the nurse. "Taste the lemon." Luka used his tongue. He thought it would taste sweet like orange juice. He took a little lick. His whole face scrunched up. "Sour!" he said. "So sour!"

"Does my tongue always know?" Luka asked. "It knew today," said the nurse. She gave him water. Luka drank it all. Then he put the sticker on his shirt. It was a gold fish that looked like it could swim in the sea. On the way home, Luka waved the lemon slice at his mom. "Taste it," he said. "It is sour." His mom took a tiny bite and made a funny face too.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Jordan sat at the big table. His whole family was there. Grandma was there too. The restaurant had a huge screen on the wall. A big game was on. Jordan wanted to cheer like the big kids.

The blue team ran fast. Jordan jumped up. "Go blue team!" he shouted. He clapped and clapped. But then everyone at the table went quiet. Uncle Max laughed. "Jordan, we like the red team!" Jordan's face turned warm. He had clapped for the wrong team.

Then the red team scored a goal. Everyone stood up and cheered. They clapped so loud. Jordan saw what made them cheer. So he stood up too. He clapped his hands and yelled, "Go red team!" Grandma gave him a high five. Jordan cheered loudest of all.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Liam stood in the school computer lab. A tablet sat on the big table. He wanted to draw a big sun on it. He did not know how to begin.

Miss Ada showed him the round button. Liam pressed it with one finger. He waited. The screen lit up. Liam clapped his hands. "I made it wake up!" he said.

Miss Ada tapped the little paint pot. The drawing app opened. Liam picked yellow. He drew a big round sun on the screen. Then he drew wiggly rays. The tablet felt smooth and warm in his hands.

Time to put it away. Liam picked up the tablet with one hand. It tipped and slid. His tummy jumped. He caught it just in time. "Hold it with two hands," said Miss Ada. Liam held it with two hands, one on each side. He held it tight. The tablet did not tip. It did not fall. It sat safe and still.

Liam walked slowly to the shelf. He set the tablet down soft as a kitten. Miss Ada smiled and pushed the button. The screen went dark. Liam waved at the sleeping tablet. "Bye bye, sun," he said.

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Madison stood at the running track. Her dad held out a red beanbag. "Throw it in the hoop," he said. Madison looked at her friend Nina. She threw the beanbag. It fell on the grass. It did not go in the hoop.

"Try again," said Nina. Madison looked at the hoop. She kept looking at it. She threw the beanbag. Plip! It went right in. "My eyes helped me!" said Madison. Her dad clapped his hands.

Then Dad rolled a big ball to her. "What if it's too big?" asked Madison. "Hold it with both hands," said Dad. The ball came near. Madison held out both hands. She caught it! She stood up straight like a tall pig statue by the fence. Then she threw the beanbag again, still looking at the hoop. In it went. "Again!" said Madison.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Arlo woke up and put on his shoes. He was ready for school. He ran to the window. Everything outside was white.

"No school today," said Mom. "It is a snow day. A snow day is a day when school is closed because of snow."

Arlo looked outside. "Can I touch it?" he asked.

"Put on your boots," said Mom. She helped him tie the laces tight. His pet dog, Biscuit, barked at the door.

Arlo stepped into the backyard. The snow was cold on his hands. His boots sank in. He made a footprint. Biscuit stepped next to it and made a paw print. Two prints side by side!

Arlo found his red sled. He pulled it up the small hill. He sat down and pushed. The sled did not move. He pushed again. Still nothing.

Then he wiggled to the top of the snowy slope. He sat and slid. Whoosh! He went fast down the hill. The snow made him slide!

"Again!" said Arlo. He climbed up and slid down. Up and down, over and over. Biscuit ran beside him every time.

Mom called from the door. "Hot cocoa is ready."

Arlo held the warm cup with both hands. He looked at his hill. "Snow day is the best day," he said. Biscuit licked the air and wagged his tail.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Leon went to the hair salon with Mama. It was his first haircut. The hairdresser was named Nan. She had a big chair and shiny scissors.

Leon climbed up into the big chair. Nan put a soft cape on him. Then Leon saw the fish tank. Three orange fish were swimming in it. One fish went round and round. Leon turned his head to see the fish. Snip! went the scissors, too long on one side.

"Hold still like a statue," said Nan, smiling. "Sitting very still helps me cut your hair neatly." Leon looked at the fish one more time. Then he sat very still, like a statue. He counted the fish in his head. One fish, two fish, three fish. Snip, snip, snip. Nan cut all around his head.

Mama held his hand the whole time. At last Nan took off the cape. Leon looked in the mirror. His hair was short and neat. "I see a little rainbow!" said Nan, pointing at the shiny scissors catching the light. Leon laughed. He was a tired, happy boy. Mama picked him up and hugged him tight. "Home now," she said, "to cook your supper."

story:
Owen sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. He did not want to be there. He was a little grumpy.

"Open wide," said Doctor Amy. Owen opened his mouth. The doctor looked in with a light. "You used your eyes to see," she said. "Good job."

Doctor Amy tapped Owen's knee. His leg jumped up all by itself. Owen laughed. "It moved!" he said.

Next she whispered near his ear. "Can you hear me?" Owen nodded. His ears worked too.

Then she held out a little stick. "Breathe in through your nose." Owen sniffed. "It smells like bread!" he said. His tummy made a hungry sound.

At home, Mom said, "Take off your shoes. Let's go in the yard." Owen pulled off his shoes and socks.

He stepped on the grass. His bare toes wiggled. "It tickles!" he said. "My feet feel it!"

Owen ran in a circle. He stomped and the soft grass squished. He stopped and looked back at his feet.

"I made a grass path," he said. "My feet did that!"

He stepped again. The grass bent down under his toes. He laughed and laughed.

"Look, Mom! My feet can feel the grass. And my feet can squish it too!"

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Anna sat at Grandma's table. The bowls were hot. Grandma had stirred the soup, and Mom had carried it over. Anna picked up her spoon. She took a big bite.

Then she looked up. Everyone else was sitting still. Their hands were folded. Nobody was eating. "We say thank-you first," said Grandma. "Many families say a thank-you before they start eating." Anna put her spoon down. She folded her hands too.

Grandma lit a little candle. She was the grown-up, so she held the match. "Thank you for the soup," Grandma said. "Thank you for the bread," said Mom. Anna wanted a turn. "Thank you for the cow," she said. "The cow helped make the milk!" Everyone smiled.

Grandma pointed at Anna. "Your turn was the best one," she said. Then Grandma blew out the candle. The smoke went up in a thin line. Anna watched it curl and vanish. "Now we eat," said Grandma. Anna took her spoon again. The soup was still warm.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Edouard wanted to read the pet book. It had a soft red cover and it smelled like paper. He opened the book. But he started at the back page. He ran his finger from the right side of the page. The picture looked all jumbled.

His teacher Ms. Lily sat down next to him. "Let me help you," she said. She put his finger at the left side of the page. "Start here." Edouard slid his finger from left to right. One word, two words, three words. "The... dog... runs," he said. He held the book tight in his lap. The words made the picture make sense.

"Did I read it?" Edouard asked. "Yes, you did," said Ms. Lily. Edouard turned to the next page. He began at the left side all by himself.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Claire wants to paint at daycare. Today the paint is all used up. "We will get more paint tomorrow," says Miss Ana. Claire sighs. Tomorrow feels far away.

Yesterday Claire played a game outside. But today is a cloudy day. Miss Ana says, "We can play inside now. And soon we will have a snack." Soon. What does soon mean? Claire waits. She builds a tower. She reads a book. Then the snack table comes out.

"See?" says Miss Ana. "Soon means in a little while." Claire eats her crackers. The wait was not long at all. After snack, Miss Ana brings out new crayons. "Soon we can draw too," she says. Claire smiles and waits. Soon is easy now. "Crackers first," says Claire. "Drawing later."

story:
Zoey sat on the rug at daycare. She had cardboard, tape, and a big want. She wanted to build a toy car for the class fish rug. "My car can give the fish a ride," she said. First she cut four squares. Four square wheels, one for each side. She taped them on and gave the car a pull. The car bumped. It stopped. It would not roll. Why not?

Ben rolled by on a truck. His truck had round wheels. Round like a circle. Zoey looked at her square wheels. Then she looked at his circle wheels. Hmm. Could that be it? She asked Miss Pam for help with the scissors. Miss Pam held the scissors and cut four circles. Zoey taped them on herself. Round wheels, one for each side.

Zoey pulled the car again. It rolled! It rolled all the way across the rug. "Look, look!" she said. Ben put his fish on top. The fish rode and rode. "You were brave to try again," said Miss Pam. Zoey smiled and gave the car one more pull. Around and around the rug it went, riding the happy fish home.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Elizabeth was at daycare. It was snack time. Miss Jo put green peas on every plate.

Tommy looked at his peas. "Yuck!" he shouted. Miss Jo gave him a sad little frown. Nobody clapped for Tommy.

Then Mia looked at her peas. She folded her hands. "No, thank you," she said. Miss Jo smiled big. "Of course, Mia. Here are carrots instead."

Elizabeth wanted carrots too. She held her breath. "No, thank you," she said, straight and tall, like a small queen.

"Carrots for Elizabeth!" said Miss Jo.

After snack, Elizabeth pretended her carrot was a butterfly. One orange wing, two orange wings. "Please fly to me," she said. The carrot flew up, up, up.

"Thank you, butterfly," said Elizabeth. "Thank you."

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Alexander stood at the bus stop with Mama. He had on his blue coat. The zipper was open. "I can do it," he said. He pulled the zipper up, up, up. Then it slid back down. He tried again. This time the zipper stayed. "I win!" said Alexander.

Little drops began to fall. Drip, drip, on his nose. "Oh no," said Alexander. "Rain." Then he felt something on his coat. It was a soft part at the top. What could it be? "That is your hood," said Mama. "The hood is the part of a coat you can pull up over your head." Alexander pulled it up. It covered his head like a turtle shell.

The rain went drip, drip, drip. Alexander stayed dry. He looked up at the hood. "Did you keep me dry?" he asked. The bus came. Alexander climbed in, not wet at all. His hands were tired from the zipper, but he smiled. "My hood works," he said.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Olivier gave him a big hug at the door. On Monday, Grandpa said, "Let's go to the park." Olivier ran ahead on the little path.

At the park, Olivier found a sign. It had a duck on it. "What does the sign say?" he asked. Grandpa read it out loud. It said ducks like bread crumbs. Olivier looked at his bread. "Who made this bread?" he asked. "I did," said Grandpa. "It is my special bread. My mother taught me. We made it together when I was small."

"Can I learn too?" asked Olivier. "Yes," said Grandpa. "Let's cook it tomorrow." So on Tuesday they stood in the kitchen. Olivier helped pour the flour. He stirred the sticky dough. Grandpa put the pan in the hot oven. Olivier stayed back and watched. Soon the bread smelled warm and good.

On Wednesday they took the new loaf to the park. Olivier broke off little crumbs. He dropped them by the pond. The ducks came swimming fast. One duck splashed with her feet. Olivier laughed. "Grandpa, your bread makes ducks come!" he said. Grandpa smiled. "And now you can make it too," he said. Olivier threw one more crumb, and the biggest duck gobbled it up.

story:

Eleanor slid down the slide. Her hands felt the smooth metal. She heard a dog bark with her ears. She saw a red kite up high. She smelled flowers with her nose.

Then Eleanor sniffed the air. "I smell dinner, Grandma! It is soup!" Grandma laughed. "We can smell dinner before we see it. Good nose." They walked home fast. In the kitchen, Daddy stirred the big pot. Grandma gave Eleanor a small taste from a cool spoon. "Soup!" Eleanor said. It was warm and good. Daddy filled her bowl.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Henri sat at the big table in the community hall. His grandma sat next to him. Bowls of soup were coming down the long table. Henri picked up his spoon.

Then everyone at the table reached out their hands. Hands went from person to person, all around. Henri held his spoon tight. His hand could not hold a spoon and a hand too.

Grandma smiled at him. "We hold hands while we say the blessing," she said. Henri put his spoon down on the table. It made a little click. Now his hand was free. He took grandma's hand on one side. He took a kind man's hand on the other side.

Everyone closed their eyes. Grandma said the blessing out loud. Her voice was soft and thick like warm honey. The soup smelled good. Outside the window, a green hill sat under the sky.

Then hands let go. Henri picked his spoon back up. He ate his soup, bite by bite. Grandma gave him bread. "Good job, Henri," she said. Henri smiled and took another big sip.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Sofia lived by the sea. The beach was big and sandy. But today she was going somewhere new. Today she was going to the pool!

Sofa grabbed her furry towel. Mama helped her carry her swim bag. They walked past the sand and the waves. Soon they saw the pool. It was bright blue and shiny. Sofia jumped up and down. "I want to swim right now!" she said.

A boy was standing by the pool. He was dripping wet. Sofia ran to jump in too. A lifeguard called out, "Stop! Take a shower first." Sofia stopped fast. "A shower?" she asked. "Yes," said the boy. "Many pools ask swimmers to take a shower before getting in." So Sofia ran to the little shower. The water went splish splash. Then she skipped back to the pool.

"Can I jump in now?" Sofia asked. "Yes, you can!" said Mama. Sofia held Mama's hand. She kicked her legs in the water. "Look at me!" she cried. "I am swimming!" The water went splash, splash, splash.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Bennett held his swim bag. He was at the pool with Dad. Today he would learn to swim.

The changing room floor was wet. Bennett saw it shine. Why did it shine like that? He wanted to find out.

Bennett started to run to the pool door. "Walk, please," said Dad. "Wet floors around a pool are slippery, so people walk instead of run."

Bennett stopped his feet. He took little steps. Walk, walk, walk. His feet did not slide at all. Then he looked at Dad's feet. Dad walked too. Dad's feet did not slide either.

A big kid ran past them. His feet went slip, slip, slip. He wobbled like a jelly. A grown-up held his arm and said, "Walk, please."

Bennett kept walking. All the people in the hall walked. Nobody slid. Nobody fell.

He got to the pool door. The water was blue and bright. Bennett looked up at Dad.

"Everyone is walking," said Bennett. "I am walking too."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandma was coming to stay for a whole week! Anna waited in the kitchen by the window. She counted the things on the table. One cup for Grandma. One cup for Anna. Two cups!

A car pulled up. Grandma was here! Anna ran to the door. She wanted to hug Grandma. But Grandma had so many bags. Her arms were full. No room for a hug.

"Hello, Grandma!" said Anna. She waved her hand up high. Grandma put down one bag. She waved back. "Hello, Anna!" said Grandma.

Then the bags were inside. Grandma's arms were free at last. "Now I can hug you," said Grandma. The hug was big and warm.

They made toast together. Mom held the knife and cut it. Anna ripped a paper napkin into pieces for their messy crumbs. Anna counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four!"

"That was my best hello ever," said Anna, waving again.

story:

Brielle ran out to the grass. The wind puffed her cheeks. Then the wind pulled her hat. Off it went, fast across the yard! Brielle chased it. The hat rolled like a wheel. Her dog Max ran too, his nose sniffing the air.

The hat stopped by the bush. Brielle picked it up. She hugged it tight. Then she put it back on her head. The wind came again. Off went the hat again! Brielle laughed. "Silly wind," she said.

Brielle held the hat with both hands. She carried it like a little bowl. The wind could not take it now. Mom came out with her own hat on. "That wind is strong," said Mom.

Brielle and Max walked to meet Mom at the gate. The wind tickled Brielle's hair. "It can blow my hat," said Brielle. "But not today." She sat down in the soft grass and held her hat on her lap.

story:
Riley went to the park with her dad. The wind was blowing. It puffed her hair all around. Sand flew up from the sandbox. A little bit went toward her face. Riley blinked fast. The sand did not get in her eyes.

"Why did I blink?" she wondered. She looked in her dad's little mirror. She saw tiny hairs on her eyelids. "Dad, what are these little hairs?" she asked. "Those are your eyelashes," said Dad. "Eyelashes help keep dust and bits of dirt out of your eyes."

Riley wanted to see more things. She used her eyes to watch a red kite go up. She used her ears to hear it snap in the wind. She used her nose to smell popcorn popping. Dad bought some, and she used her tongue to taste the salty bits.

Then Riley touched the grass with her fingers. It was soft and a little wet. A ladybug landed right on her hand! "Hello, little friend," she said. The wind blew again. Sand flew by her face once more. Riley blinked, and her eyelashes caught the sand. Her eyes stayed clean and dry. She laughed and blinked again, just to feel them work.

story:
Elliot wanted to have a tea party. He wanted one so, so much. He set his teddy bear on a little chair. He set his rubber duck on another chair. "Tea time!" he called.

Then Elliot had a problem. The teapot was empty. Mom was busy, and the tea things lived up high. His shoulders drooped. How could he have tea with no tea?

Then he looked at the empty cups. He picked one up and tipped the empty teapot over it. He made a pouring sound. "Glug, glug, glug." Nothing came out, but he said, "There! Full!"

He handed a cup to the duck. "Here is your tea, duck." He handed a cup to teddy. "Careful, it's pretend hot!" He blew on his own cup. Then he took a big pretend sip. "Mmm. Juicy tea," he said, and he giggled.

Mom peeked around the door. "May I have tea too?" she asked. Elliot poured her an empty cup, glug glug glug. "Careful, it's pretend hot!" he said. Mom blew on it and sipped. "Best tea ever," she said. Elliot clapped. "More tea, everyone!" he shouted. "Glug, glug, glug."

story:

At the car, Mom opened the bag. There was a small surprise inside. A tiny sticker of a happy apple sat on top. "For you," said Mom. Isaiah put it on his shirt. "I said please," he said. Then he took a big, crunchy bite.

Grayson was going on a big trip. The car was packed full. "Camping today!" Daddy yelled.

The car went up a hill. Then it went down the hill. Grayson counted the trees. "One tree, two trees, three trees!"

Then the car stopped. Daddy made a sad face. "I think we took a wrong turn," he said. The road was small and bumpy. No campsite was here.

Mommy held up a big paper with roads on it. "Look, this is a map," she said. "It shows roads and places. It can help us find the way."

Grayson leaned over the seat. He saw little lines and dots. "Is our campsite on there?" he asked. Mommy pointed to a spotted dot. "Yes! Right there."

Grayson put his finger on the dot. "Go this way!" he said. Daddy turned the car around. They found the big road again. One road, two roads, three roads.

Soon they saw tents and a lake. "We made it!" Grayson yelled. He jumped out and hugged his spotted teddy bear. "The map found us!"

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Charlotte got a new bike for her birthday. She loved to ride it fast. But one day her long hair got in her eyes. She fell off her bike. Her legs felt weak and she sat on the grass.

"Mama, my hair is in my way," said Charlotte.

"Then it is time for your first haircut," said Mama.

They went to the barbershop. Charlotte saw the big chair. She saw the scissors. The scissors looked sharp.

"Will the scissors hurt me?" she asked.

"Cutting hair does not hurt," said the barber. "You will see."

Charlotte climbed into the big chair. The chair went up and up. The barber snipped one little snip.

"That is all?" said Charlotte. "I did not feel it!"

She watched in the mirror. Snip, snip, snip. Little pieces of hair fell down. They rolled off the cape like tiny curls of paper. It did not hurt at all.

"More," said Charlotte. "You can do more."

The barber smiled. He cut and cut. Soon Charlotte had short, bouncy hair. It was out of her eyes.

At home, Charlotte rode her bike again. Her hair stayed back. No more falls.

"I love my haircut," she said.

story:
Today was a big day at Luke's house. Grandma was making challah bread. It was bread just for the holiday. "Can I taste it now?" Luke asked. "Not yet, little one," said Grandma. "First we make it."

Luke stood on his step stool. Grandma gave him dough. "Push it down," she said. Luke pushed. The dough went flat! Then Grandma showed him how to fold it over. Luke folded and folded. The dough looked like a little nest now.

The bread went into the oven. Grandma put it in, not Luke. The oven was hot. They waited and waited. Luke's tummy made a growl. At last the bread came out, big and gold. Luke's hands were empty no more. He held a warm piece. He took a bite. "Mmm!" said Luke. "It tastes like a happy day!"

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Hailey and Grandma went to the grocery store. It was cold outside. Grandma handed Hailey her red coat.

"Can I do it myself?" asked Hailey. "Yes, you can," said Grandma.

Hailey pushed both arms into one sleeve. The coat wiggled like a worm. She laughed and fell over on the soft bench. "That is not right!" she said. Her arms were stuck together in one long sleeve. She could not even pick up her juice to drink it.

Grandma smiled. "Try again, Hailey."

Hailey pulled her arms out. Then she put one arm in one sleeve. She put her other arm in the other sleeve. The coat felt just right now. She pulled the zipper up, up, up. Click! It was zipped all by herself.

"Is it true I did it all alone?" asked Hailey. "All alone," said Grandma.

Outside, they walked past the garden by the store. A little brown dog wore a tiny coat too. "Look, Grandma!" said Hailey. "He knows the sleeve trick too!"

activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Henri sat on the train with Mama. The seat was bumpy under him. He held his cup of milk with two hands. "Where are we going?" he asked. "To the beach," said Mama. Henri looked out the window. Trees went by fast. Then the trees stopped, and there was sand. There was the big blue sea.

At the beach, Henri saw the water. The waves went up and down. "Waves!" he shouted. He wanted to splash right now. He ran to the wet sand. But Mama called, "Wait for me, Henri." Henri stopped. He stood and watched. A wave came in and touched his toes. Then he stepped back to Mama.

"Why do I wait?" Henri asked. "Little ones go near the water with a grown-up watching," said Mama. She took his hand. Her hand was warm and strong. His own legs felt weak after the long train ride. Now Mama was right beside him.

Together they walked to the water. A big wave came. Splash! It went over their feet. Henri laughed. "Again!" he said. Another wave came, and Mama held his hand tight.

story:
Hudson sat at the little table. He wanted to paint green grass. He looked in the paint cups. Red, yellow, blue. No green paint at all.

Hudson frowned at his paper. "I need green for the grass," he said. Miss Amy came over. She waited with him. She did not hurry him.

Hudson put his brush in the yellow cup. He painted a big yellow blob. Then he put his brush in the blue cup. He painted blue right on top of the yellow. He swirled the brush around and around.

The blob turned green. Hudson stopped. He looked and looked. "It's green!" he said. He painted tall green grass all the way up the paper. Then he painted a purple flower next to the grass.

At tidy-up time, Hudson sang a little song while he put the brushes away. He scratched an itch on his nose. There was a small green spot on his nose too. Miss Amy smiled at him. "Green grass boy," she said.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Alice sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump over the road. She was going to see her friend Ben.

"I want Ben now," Alice said.

"Not now, Alice," said Mama. "Ben is not home today. We go tomorrow."

Alice looked out the window. A cow stood in a field. "Cow, I see Ben today," Alice said in a small mouth voice. The cow just ate grass.

"Yesterday we played at home," said Mama. "Today we ride in the car. Tomorrow we see Ben."

"Now?" asked Alice.

"Later," said Mama. "First you sleep. Then it is tomorrow."

Alice held her heavy bag. It had a toy bunny inside. She hugged the bunny tight.

"Sleep, bunny," she said. "Then tomorrow comes."

The car went on and on. Alice's eyes got small, then shut. She slept in her seat.

The sun came up. Alice woke up in her little bed. "Is it tomorrow?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mama. "Today is the day after yesterday."

Alice clapped her hands. She grabbed the bunny and ran to the car.

The car stopped at Ben's house. Ben waved at the door.

"Ben!" Alice called. "I slept, and now it is tomorrow!"

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Everly wanted her red blocks. But the block box was in the car. It was dark outside. "Can I get my blocks now?" she asked. "Later," said Mama. "First we have dinner, then later we get blocks."

Everly ate her dinner. She tasted the lemon in her water. "Sour!" she said, and made a funny face. Mama laughed. Everly drank more water.

"Is it later yet?" Everly asked. "Not yet," said Mama. "Now we wash hands." Everly washed her hands. "Is it later now?" "Not yet. Now we put on pajamas." Everly put on her pajamas.

Papa went out to the car with a flashlight. Everly waited at the door. Now she heard the car door open. Now she heard Papa's feet on the steps. Now Papa set the block box down. "It is later," said Papa.

Everly sat on her bed. She stacked one block, then two, then three. The tower went up and up. "I got them later," she said. She yawned big. Mama tucked the blocks under the bed. "Blocks again tomorrow," said Mama. Everly closed her eyes and held her bear tight.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Ellie sat at the dinner table. She looked at her plate. There was rice and a piece of broccoli. The broccoli looked like a little green boat.

"I want pancakes," said Ellie. "We had pancakes yesterday."

"Yes," said Mom. "Yesterday is gone. Today is rice day."

Ellie felt upset. Her bottom lip went down. "I want pancakes now."

Dad sat down next to her. "Pancakes are for morning," he said. "Tomorrow, when you wake up, we will eat breakfast. Good morning, Ellie. Pancakes for you."

Ellie thought about that. Morning was when she woke up. Morning was breakfast time. She could almost see it. She would open her eyes. The sun would be in her window. She would smell pancakes.

"Okay," said Ellie. "Tomorrow morning, pancakes. Today, rice."

She picked up her fork. She pushed the rice around. The broccoli boat sailed on top. "Look, Dad. The boat is sailing."

"Now we eat dinner," said Mom. "Later, we will wash hands and brush teeth."

"Now dinner," said Ellie. "Later, teeth. Tomorrow, pancakes and morning."

"That's right," said Dad.

Ellie took a big bite of rice. Then she made the little green boat sail right into her mouth. "Next stop, tomorrow!" she said.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Dylan ran to the park with his red truck. The sun was warm. The weather was just right for playing outside. He felt so excited. His tummy was full of breakfast, and his truck bed was full of little stones.

Dylan pushed the truck across the grass. Vroom, vroom. Then he heard a loud thump. A boy named Sam had tripped by the slide. Sam sat on the ground. His face looked sad, and then he looked angry at his shoes. He rubbed his knee.

Dylan felt a little scared for Sam. He walked over slowly. "Are you okay?" he asked. Sam looked up. His sad face began to change. He nodded his head. "Yes," Sam said. "That helps. Thank you." Dylan held out his hand. Sam took it and stood up.

Then Sam pushed the truck too. Vroom, vroom, they went, side by side across the warm green grass.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Anthony woke up early. "Is it library day?" he asked. Mom smiled. "Yes. It is today. Today is the day happening right now." Anthony clapped. "Today, today, today!"

At the library, Anthony saw the big clock. "Is now library time?" he asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Now is this minute. Later we will read at home." Anthony ran to the shelf. One red book, two blue books, three little books. He counted them all.

"Can we get the book again?" he asked. "The bear book?" Mom nodded. "We had it yesterday. Yesterday is the day that is done. Today we have it now." Anthony hugged the bear book. "What about tomorrow?" he asked. "Tomorrow is the day that comes next," said Mom. "Tomorrow we will read it again." Anthony smiled. "Today, tomorrow, and cake at home?" "Later," said Mom. "First, books." Anthony carried his three books all by himself.

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Sofia sat in the car with her mama. They were going to the dentist. It was her very first time. "My tummy feels funny," said Sofia. "That is called worried," said Mama. "You can hold my hand." Sofia squeezed Mama's fingers. One, two, three squeezes. The car seat was warm. The window smelled like sunshine.

At the dentist, a kind lady looked in Sofia's mouth. "How can you see behind my teeth?" asked Sofia. The dentist held up a tiny mirror on a handle. "Watch," she said. She put it near Sofia's back teeth. Sofia saw her own teeth in the little mirror. One tooth, two teeth, three white teeth!

After that, Sofia got to hold the tiny mirror herself. She reached up and saw her ear in it. She giggled. "Mama, look! The little mirror shows everything!" In the car going home, she held a sticker on her knee. "The dentist was nice," said Sofia. "Can we count my teeth again tomorrow?"
